The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Exercise: Exercise' is not clinically well aligned with the rest of the profile. The other selected strategies are cognitive perseveration focused on the trauma and pre-trauma self, while the threat and memory items emphasize hypervigilance, nighttime fear, and fragmented sensory/emotional memory. Avoiding exercise addresses a different symptom domain and, given the formulation, is hard to connect plausibly to the active Memory/Threat/Negative Appraisals pathways driving maladaptive strategies.

vignette:
Fatima is a 53-year-old woman of Lebanese descent, married, and currently serving as a ship captain operating cargo routes along the Gulf Coast. She presented for psychological assessment describing herself as exhausted in a way that sleep no longer touched, and it took several sessions before the full shape of what she carried began to emerge.

Fatima grew up in a household governed by fear. Her father, a man whose rages arrived without warning and departed without apology, beat her regularly from the time she was perhaps five or six years old until she left for university at eighteen. The violence was not chaotic - it had a terrible orderliness to it. He would come to her room at night, and the sound of footsteps in the hallway, the specific creak of a door being tested, became the architecture of dread. She learned to lie still in the dark and listen, to parse the quality of silence for what it concealed. Extended family knew, or suspected, and said nothing. The mosque community, to which her mother clung as a social lifeline, offered no intervention. Fatima left Lebanon as soon as she could and built a life defined by forward motion - maritime studies, certifications, command. For decades, the strategy worked well enough.

The symptoms she describes now did not announce themselves all at once. In her late forties, following her mother's death and a return to Beirut for the funeral, something shifted. She found herself lying awake on the ship at night, listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering her quarters - a habit so automatic she barely recognized it as unusual until her first officer commented that she seemed always to be waiting for something. She cannot relax even when she knows, rationally, that she is safe; the body simply refuses the information. Nighttime is categorically different from day. On deck in full sun, surrounded by her crew, she functions with the authority and composure her position demands. But after dark, even anchored in a familiar port, the sense of safety drains away and something older takes its place.

Her memories of her father's abuse come to her in fragments - visual images, mostly, frozen and specific: the particular angle of light from a hallway, the pattern on a pillowcase, a hand raised. Sometimes these images arrive with their full emotional charge intact but with no narrative context, a wave of terror or shame that seems to come from nowhere and belongs to nothing she can consciously name. At other times she can review what happened with a strange, dissociated clarity, as though reading a case file about someone else - the facts present, the feeling entirely absent. She finds both states disturbing in different ways.

What Fatima dwells on most, in the long watches of the night, is the question of prevention. She returns again and again to the people who knew and did nothing - the aunts, the neighbors, the religious figures her mother trusted - and she has come to believe, with a quiet and settled certainty, that institutions designed to protect are fundamentally unreliable. She also mourns a version of herself she believes existed before the abuse shaped her - a girl who could trust, who belonged somewhere, who did not experience her own cultural community as a place of abandonment. That lost connection is not abstract to her. When Lebanese colleagues invite her to community events, she declines. She has told herself she simply does not have the time.

She tries hard not to think about any of it. The effort is constant and largely unsuccessful, and she is aware, at some level, that it is costing her something.

What finally brought Fatima to seek help was a conversation with her husband, who told her gently that she had not seemed present with him in over a year. She had not realized he had been counting. She came to the first appointment hoping to be told there was something specific and fixable, and what she fears most is the opposite - that this is simply who she has become, and that the girl who might have been otherwise is genuinely, permanently gone.
